content: 1. Physical symptoms that suggest illness or injury but cannot be fully explained by a general medical condition or the direct effects of a substance, as well as other psychosomatic conditions, should be assessed comprehensively. Full support from the Global Reference Centre (GRC) is recommended. 2. Referral and support for the management of psychotic disorders should be provided with full GRC support. 3. Comprehensive care and support should be extended to individuals dealing with substance use, including alcohol and illicit drugs, with full GRC support. 4. Management of substance withdrawal should include appropriate referral and support, with full GRC support. 5. Data at the population level should be utilized effectively for planning school health programs, including the collection, analysis, and use of data on school health service utilization and quality of care. This is essential for monitoring performance, supporting quality improvement, and facilitating evaluation and planning. 6. Protocols should be established for school health services to provide essential services during complex emergencies, such as outbreaks of cholera, conjunctivitis, coronaviruses, dysentery, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, influenza, meningococcal disease, rubella, scabies, scarlet fever, tuberculosis, typhoid, and varicella. Partial GRC support is available for these efforts. 7. Support should be provided for school policies addressing chronic conditions, hygiene, and nutrition, as well as mental health promotion, including listening services and pre-counseling. Partial GRC support is available. 8. Prevention of adolescent pregnancy, school violence, and substance use should be prioritized, with partial GRC support. 9. School policies should address bullying, harassment, and anaphylaxis prevention and response, with partial GRC support. 10. Nutritional content of school feeding programs, food safety inspections, and community engagement to create a healthy school environment should be supported, with partial GRC support. 11. Promotion of responsible parenting skills for all students should be encouraged, with support from WHO. 12. Screening for students at risk of poor mental health outcomes or those requiring monitoring or referral should be implemented, with support from WHO. 13. Immunizations and mass drug administration for diseases such as cholera, dengue, hepatitis A, meningococcal disease, rabies, and typhoid should be conducted with full GRC support. 14. Encouraging children to adopt healthy habits, such as adequate sleep, regular meals, physical activity, social engagement, and avoidance of alcohol, drugs, and nicotine, should be emphasized. Development of interpersonal skills, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and stress management should also be supported, with full GRC support. 15. Counseling on nutrition, physical activity, and management plans, if needed, should be provided, with partial GRC support. 16. Training school staff on first aid, hygiene promotion, and injury prevention should be prioritized, with support from WHO. 17. Screening for Type II diabetes, tuberculosis, neglected tropical diseases (e.g., Chagas disease), and COVID-19 should be conducted, with support from WHO. 18. Iron, folic acid, and other micronutrient supplementation should be provided, with full GRC support. 19. Referral and support for voluntary medical male circumcision should be available, with full GRC support. 20. WHO guidance identifies interventions unsuitable for inclusion in school health services (SHS), such as universal screening for maltreatment by a parent or guardian and exposure to intimate-partner violence. These interventions may be supported in other healthcare settings but are not recommended for SHS. 21. Dissemination of the WHO guideline on SHS is being conducted through printed publications, online resources, and a network of international partners, including WHO offices, ministries of education and health, universities, and NGOs. Digital technology will also be explored for dissemination and implementation. 22. National adaptation of the WHO guideline on SHS is expected, with Member States tailoring recommendations and interventions to their local context and feasibility. WHO regional and country offices will assist in these processes. 23. SHS programs should align with broader national health strategies, focusing on evaluating and improving existing programs to make them more comprehensive and evidence-based. 24. Collaboration between the health and education sectors is critical for effective SHS implementation. This includes coordination with other sectors, such as social services and water and sanitation, as well as engagement with parents and the community. 25. SHS can be delivered through school-based or school-linked services, with trained health workers collaborating closely with education staff and other health and social service providers. 26. The primary beneficiaries of SHS are students, but their families can also contribute to informing and monitoring SHS through participatory research and other activities.
